episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Friday, May eighth, twenty twenty-six. And here's who is innovating in higher education today.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Leading off today's Innovation Pulse, a Columbia University research team scanned ninety-seven million references across two and a half million biomedical papers and found more than four thousand citations that do not exist in scientific databases. The findings, published this week in The Lancet, show fabricated citations climbed from four per ten thousand papers in twenty twenty-three to fifty-seven per ten thousand by early this year. That represents a twelve-fold increase in just over two years.

The sharpest rise began in mid-twenty twenty-four, coinciding with widespread adoption of generative A.I. writing tools. Associate professor Maxim Topaz, who led the Columbia School of Nursing study, said this discovery directly impacts patients because medical professionals make treatment decisions based on clinical guidelines. A clinician or guideline developer has no way of knowing that the evidence they are relying on does not exist.

The audit found extreme cases, including one paper with eighteen of thirty references fabricated. Some fake citations have already spread to systematic reviews that underpin clinical guidelines. At the time of the audit, more than ninety-eight percent of affected papers had not received any publisher action. The Columbia team made their A.I.-assisted verification tool available for other institutions and publishers to use, demonstrating how the same technology contributing to the problem can help identify fabricated references at scale.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Also in Insights and Trends, Stanford University merged its Human-Centered A.I. Institute with Stanford Data Science on May fourth, putting more than four hundred affiliated scholars under unified governance. The combined institute gives researchers across disciplines access to the Marlowe high-performance computing cluster and sixty million dollars in pooled grant funding. The merger also unifies the industry affiliates network and the early scholar fellowship program.

Computer scientist James Landay leads the combined institute. Fei-Fei Li, who co-founded HAI in twenty nineteen, takes a new university-wide advisory role alongside John Hennessy on the advisory council. Landay said this is not just a stronger institute but a new model for how a university organizes A.I. and data science to have real impact in the world. The restructuring follows similar moves at other research universities working to coordinate A.I. efforts that had grown across multiple departments.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Beyond Ed news, Hawaii's legislature gave final approval this week to Senate Bill three thousand one, requiring conversational A.I. platforms to disclose when users are interacting with artificial intelligence rather than a human. The Artificial Intelligence Disclosure and Safety Act now goes to the governor.

The legislation establishes safeguards for minors, including protections against manipulative engagement techniques and sexually explicit content. Beginning January twenty twenty-eight, operators will submit annual reports to the Department of Health outlining crisis intervention protocols. Representative Trish La Chica said what sets Hawaii's bill apart is that, unlike laws passed in some other states, it does not create broad carveouts for certain A.I. products or platforms.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Meanwhile in A.I. Workforce and Careers, the unemployment rate among recent college graduates reached five point seven percent in the fourth quarter, a four-year high, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data. Junior-level job postings fell seven percent over the past year even as more graduates entered the workforce, Scripps News reported.

The Economic Policy Institute analysis found the elevated unemployment reflects more graduates actively seeking work rather than employers cutting existing positions. Laura Ullrich, Director of Economic Research at Indeed, described the current environment as low-hire, low-fire. Survey data shows nearly nine in ten graduates express concern about A.I. affecting entry-level roles, while only one in three say college prepared them for workplace A.I. Nearly forty percent are now using A.I. tools in their job search.

<break time="1.0s"/>

And at Arizona State University, seventy-five students ranging from age eighteen to seventy completed the university's first agentic A.I. course in mid-April. The fifteen-week course, titled The Agentic Self, is one of the first university-level personal A.I. agent courses in the United States that requires no computer science or coding background, AfroTech reported.

Students built personalized A.I. agents addressing real-world problems as final projects. The top project created an agent helping Brazilian street vendors navigate a payment platform. Other projects focused on helping military veterans understand benefits and developing translation tools for African languages absent from mainstream platforms. ASU developed the course in partnership with will.i.am, who serves as Professor of Practice. A second semester is scheduled for later this year.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Thank you for joining us. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

leadStory.headline: Columbia A.I. Audit Identifies 4,046 Fabricated Citations Across 2,810 Medical Papers
leadStory.summary:
A Columbia University School of Nursing research team scanned 97.1 million references across 2.5 million biomedical papers and identified 4,046 citations that do not exist in scientific databases. The findings, published May 7 in The Lancet in a research letter titled "Fabricated citations: an audit across 2.5 million biomedical papers," show the fabrication rate climbed from 4 citations per 10,000 papers in 2023 to 57 per 10,000 by early 2026.

The audit covered papers published between January 2023 and February 2026 in PubMed Central's Open Access collection. The sharpest increase began in mid-2024, coinciding with widespread adoption of generative A.I. tools capable of producing academic-style text.

"This discovery directly impacts patients as medical professionals make treatment decisions based on clinical guidelines," said Maxim Topaz, associate professor at Columbia's School of Nursing and Data Science Institute, who led the study. "A medical professional or clinical guideline developer has no way of knowing that the evidence they are relying on does not exist."

The audit uncovered extreme cases, including one paper with 18 of 30 references fabricated. Some fake citations have already been propagated in other publications and systematic reviews that underpin clinical guidelines. At the time of the audit, 98.4 percent of affected papers had not received any publisher action.

The A.I.-assisted verification tool developed by the Columbia team demonstrates how the same technology contributing to the problem can help identify fabricated references at scale. The research team made the tool available for other institutions and publishers to use in screening submissions.
leadStory.source: The Lancet / Columbia University School of Nursing

quickHits.headline: Stanford Unifies A.I. Research Under Single Institute, Giving 400 Scholars Access to Shared Computing Power
quickHits.summary:
Stanford University merged its Human-Centered A.I. Institute with Stanford Data Science on May 4, giving more than 400 affiliated scholars across disciplines access to the Marlowe high-performance computing cluster and 60 million dollars in pooled grant funding. The combined institute operates under the Stanford HAI name.

The consolidation addresses a practical challenge: researchers in fields from medicine to law increasingly need large-scale computing resources for A.I. work, but these resources were previously split between separate programs. The merger puts the computing cluster, the industry affiliates network, and the early scholar fellowship program under unified governance.

Computer scientist James Landay leads the combined institute. Fei-Fei Li, who co-founded HAI in 2019, takes a new university-wide advisory role and joins John Hennessy as co-chair of the advisory council.

"This is not just a stronger institute," Landay said. "It is a new model for how a university organizes A.I. and data science to have real impact in the world."

Emmanuel Candès, who launched Stanford Data Science, becomes associate director for computational resources. The restructuring follows similar moves at other research universities working to coordinate A.I. efforts that had grown across multiple departments.

quickHits.headline: Hawaii Legislature Passes A.I. Disclosure Act Requiring Transparency for Minors
quickHits.summary:
Hawaii's legislature gave final approval May 7 to Senate Bill 3001, requiring conversational A.I. platforms to disclose when users are interacting with artificial intelligence rather than a human. The Artificial Intelligence Disclosure and Safety Act now goes to the governor.

The legislation establishes safeguards for minors, including protections against manipulative engagement techniques and sexually explicit content. Operators must provide tools for parents and guardians to manage screen time and account settings. Beginning January 2028, operators will submit annual reports to the Department of Health outlining crisis intervention referral activity and protocols for addressing suicidal ideation.

"What sets Hawaii's bill apart is that, unlike laws passed in some other states, it does not create broad carveouts for certain A.I. products or platforms," said Representative Trish La Chica. "In many cases, some of the A.I. tools most widely used by children are exempted from oversight before protections even begin."

Violations will be treated as unfair or deceptive acts under state law and enforced by the Department of the Attorney General and the Office of Consumer Protection.

quickHits.headline: Recent Graduate Unemployment Reaches Four-Year High at 5.7 Percent
quickHits.summary:
The unemployment rate among recent college graduates climbed to 5.7 percent in the fourth quarter, the highest level in four years, Bureau of Labor Statistics data shows. Scripps News reported that junior-level job postings fell 7 percent over the past year even as more graduates entered the workforce.

Laura Ullrich, Director of Economic Research at Indeed, described the current landscape as a low-hire, low-fire environment. Indeed data shows that 19 percent of 2025 graduates created profiles on the platform, nearly double the rate from two years earlier.

The graduates themselves are watching A.I. closely. Survey data cited by Scripps News found that 9 in 10 expressed concern about A.I. affecting entry-level work, while only 1 in 3 felt their college education prepared them for A.I. in the workplace. Nearly 40 percent reported using A.I. tools during their job search.

The Economic Policy Institute analysis found the elevated unemployment reflects more graduates actively seeking work rather than employers cutting existing positions. Keith Spencer, a career expert interviewed by Scripps News, said employers have slowed hiring as they assess how A.I. will change the roles they need to fill.

quickHits.headline: Arizona State Completes First Semester of Agentic A.I. Course Without Coding Prerequisites
quickHits.summary:
Seventy-five students ranging from age 18 to 70 completed Arizona State University's first agentic A.I. course in mid-April, one of the first university-level personal A.I. agent courses in the United States that requires no computer science or coding background. The 15-week course, titled "The Agentic Self," was offered through ASU's The GAME School.

Students built personalized A.I. agents addressing real-world problems as final projects. The top project created an agent helping Brazilian street vendors navigate a payment platform. Other projects focused on helping military veterans understand benefits and developing translation tools for African languages absent from mainstream platforms.

The course alternated between a Hollywood studio and the Tempe campus across 16 class sessions. Students explored A.I. ethics, bias elimination, and community building alongside technical implementation.

ASU developed the course in partnership with will.i.am, who serves as Professor of Practice and founded the FYI.AI platform. A second semester is scheduled for later this year. The initiative connects to will.i.am's i.am Angel Foundation, which provides STEM education to 15,000 Los Angeles high school students.
